entities.summary:
The orb, a globular object traditionally adorned with a cross, serves as a potent symbol of authority within Christian iconography, particularly during the Classical era (circa 500 BCE - 476 CE). This emblem, often associated with sovereign power, was frequently used by monarchs and church leaders across Europe and beyond, signifying their divine right to rule. Notable figures such as Charlemagne and later monarchs of the Holy Roman Empire adopted the orb in their regalia, intertwining political power with religious legitimacy.

The orb's prominence can be traced back to the Roman Empire's adoption of Christianity in the 4th century CE, under Emperor Constantine I, who sought to unify the empire under a single faith. As Christianity spread throughout Europe, the orb became an integral part of royal coronation ceremonies, often presented alongside the scepter and crown as symbols of a ruler's divine appointment. The orb was not merely decorative; it embodied the idea of a Christian universe, ordered and governed by God, and served as a reminder of the ruler's responsibility to uphold divine law.

In the centuries that followed, the orb's legacy endured, influencing the iconography of monarchies and religious institutions worldwide. Its representation evolved, becoming a standard element in various coats of arms and insignias. The orb's use in ceremonial contexts persisted into the modern era, as seen in the coronation regalia of British monarchs. As a symbol of authority, the orb resonates with the historical relationship between church and state, illustrating how religious symbolism has shaped political structures.
